newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Bodyguard-turned-deputy may rock Kremlin boat.
newsitem.headline: Bodyguard-turned-deputy may rock Kremlin boat.

text.p: Alexander Korzhakov, elected to parliament on Monday, could upset Kremlin insiders if he spills the beans on his time as President Boris Yeltsin's personal bodyguard and confidant.
In public Korzhakov was the man who opened the car door for Yeltsin, pressing a rogue strip of hair over his pate and looking warily around him as he did.
But behind the scenes he became much more than that during 11 years at Yeltsin's side.
Tennis, swimming and, some say, drinking partner of the Russian president, the 47-year-old former mechanic was a close personal friend and he controlled access to his boss.
He occasionally issued statements contradicting official policy, earning little more than a rap over the knuckles.
Fired in a purge of Kremlin hawks last June, Korzhakov alleged it was part of a plot by liberal members of the administration and hinted they would come to regret the move.

"We (ousted Kremlin officials) are meant to sink into oblivion. This is neither just nor wise because we know very important state secrets," Korzhakov said in an interview published by the German magazine Der Spiegel last year.

It was the first in a series of hints that Korzhakov had information he was ready to use. He has played his cards close to his chest, but journalists from the tabloid Litsa say they are helping him to write memoirs to be published in the West.

"If ex-presidential bodyguard Korzhakov gets the mandate, he will get his long-awaited deputy's immunity," influential television anchorman Yevgeny Kiselyov said on Sunday, referring to Russian laws which say deputies cannot be prosecuted.

"Then the compromising materials with which he has so far only threatened everybody will probably start to be published...and this will lead to a new spiral of political instability," Kiselyov said on NTV commercial television.

The history of Korzhakov's relations with Yeltsin goes back to 1985 when, a major with the KGB secret police, he was assigned to protect Yeltsin, then a junior member of the ruling Communist Party politburo.
When Yeltsin was hounded out of office by former Soviet president Mikhail Gorbachev in 1987, Korzhakov broke ranks and stayed with his boss, driving him around in his own modest car.
He stood by Yeltsin when the president defied a hardline coup against Gorbachev in 1991.

Korzhakov played tennis with Yeltsin and became a family friend. His influence grew, along with the military might of the presidential bodyguards, and the liberal media started calling him the grey eminence of the Kremlin.

In the run-up to the presidential election, he caused a scandal by saying he wanted the vote postponed. This led to a clash with liberal Anatoly Chubais, then effective head of Yeltsin's campaign and now the Kremlin chief of staff.
Korzhakov blamed Chubais for his sacking and called him a "regent" who had assumed undeserved power as Yeltsin struggled first with heart problems and, more recently, pneumonia.

He also said Yeltsin's daughter Tatyana Dyachenko was in league with Chubais and he formed an alliance with ousted former security chief Alexander Lebed, Russia's most popular politician and a leading candidate to replace Yeltsin in a future election.
This was too much for the Kremlin, which issued an order in October to strip Korzhakov of his military rank.
"After his sacking on June 20, 1996, Lieutenant-General Alexander Korzhakov has come out with a series of lies concerning the Russian president and members of his family," it said.
